text: Second of four. Same brief, same five checks, different harness. And this one is the tool most of you already have access to without buying anything new, because your employer probably already pays for it.

Before anything else, a small ritual that repeats before every build in this section, and it is worth learning once rather than watching four times. The finished project gets renamed, so it survives as a record of what that tool produced. Then the same repository is cloned again, fresh, and we are back to one file and nothing else.

That is the only way the comparison means anything. If build two starts in a folder where build one left code lying around, then what you are measuring is not the second tool, it is the mess the first one left behind.
So four folders, four records, one brief. And by the end of the day you will be able to open any of them and see exactly what that tool did with the same instructions.
GitHub Copilot is not a separate application. It lives inside Visual Studio Code, which means if you already work there, the whole of today happens without you moving house.

Now, where this one lives. And this is the part that surprises people, because Copilot is not an application you download and open. There is no Copilot on your dock. It is an extension, which means it lives inside an editor you already have.

The editor is Visual Studio Code, and it is free, and it is almost certainly the most widely used editor in the world. If you have ever had a developer look over your shoulder, this is probably what was on their screen.

And here is the detail that makes today much less frightening than it looks. Cursor, the tool we used yesterday and in the last lecture, is built on top of Visual Studio Code. Not inspired by it. Built from its actual source code, with their own features added on.

Which means the thing you are about to look at is going to feel familiar in a way that has nothing to do with you being clever. Same file tree on the left. Same tabs. Same panel at the bottom. Same keyboard shortcuts. You already know most of this room.

Hold on to that, because it is going to happen twice more today. Two of the four tools in this comparison are also built from this same editor. Once you can find your way around one of them, you can find your way around all of them, and that is a much bigger deal than any single feature any of them ships.

On the money. There is a free tier here, and it is a real one, not a seven day trial. You get an allowance of requests each month, and when it runs out you wait for the month to turn over or you pay. For what we are doing today, the free allowance is enough.

I want to flag that because it changes who this lecture is for. Everything else we compare today either costs money or has a much tighter limit. If you are following along and you only want to do one of these four builds yourself, do this one.

And I want to be exact about what we are changing between these four builds, because it is easy to lose track. The agents file is identical. The prompt is identical. The five checks are identical. What changes is the harness around the model, and nothing else.
So. Fresh folder, fresh clone of the same repository, and the same single file sitting in it. Nothing from the Cursor build carries over.
Copilot's agent lives in the chat panel on the right. Same shape as Cursor's, different furniture. There is a mode selector, and there is a model selector, and both of them matter.

The panel opens on the right, and if you were with us in the last lecture you have seen this shape already. A box to type in at the bottom. A history of the conversation above it. And two small controls that decide almost everything about what happens next.

The first control is the mode. This one calls it Agent, which means it is allowed to read your files, write new ones, and run commands, rather than just talking to you about your code. That is the whole difference between a chatbot and an agent, and it is a single dropdown.

One difference worth naming immediately. Cursor gave me a Plan mode as a separate thing I had to switch into. Copilot folds planning into the agent rather than making it a mode, so the shape of what comes back is going to be a little different.

The second control is the model, and on the free tier there is exactly one option, called Auto. Auto means the tool picks for you, and it picks based on what is fast, what is cheap, and what it thinks the job needs. You do not get a vote.

In the last lecture I made a point of choosing the model by hand, so that a difference in the result would tell us something. Here I cannot. So the honest thing to do is the next best thing, which is to read what it actually used and say it out loud.

Before we look at what came back, I want to name the model, because a comparison that hides it is not a comparison. Cursor ran this brief on its own frontier tier. Copilot, on the free plan, gives you one choice, and that choice is called Auto, which means the tool decides for you. Today, for this build, Auto picked GPT five point six Luna, and it told me so in small grey text under its own answer, along with what it charged me for it. Check that line yourself rather than trusting mine, because it will have moved by the time you watch this.

And it does tell you. Underneath every answer there is a line of small grey text with the time, the name of the model that answered, and what it cost. Most people never look at that line. Look at it. It is the only place the tool is completely straight with you about what you just spent.

That cost is measured in credits, and a credit is roughly one request. This whole build, six phases, dozens of file edits, a test suite and a browser run, came to under four credits. Which tells you the free allowance goes a lot further than you would guess from the pricing page.
And the prompt is the same four words. Go ahead and plan. Not one of them says what to build, because the file says what to build.
This is the moment that tells you whether the last two lectures were worth it. If the file is doing its job, this tool has everything it needs from four words, exactly like the last one did.

Watch what it reads before it answers. It does not go straight to the code. It looks for documentation, finds the brief, and reads that first. Nobody told it the file was there. It went looking, because looking for a brief is what these tools now do.
That is the payoff for the last two lectures, and it arrives in about four seconds. Everything we wrote into that file is now doing work inside a tool we had never opened when we wrote it.
Now the plan. Six phases, and I am not going to read you all of it, because the interesting part is not the phases.

The interesting part is the last line under each one. Success, colon, and then something you could actually check. The app starts and renders a page. Each required action works. The board feels complete on desktop and on mobile. Browser checks pass with nothing overlapping.

Those lines are the difference between a plan and a to-do list. A to-do list tells you what it intends to do. A success check tells you how it will know it worked, which means it has committed to something you can hold it to later.
And it wrote them because the brief told it to. That single instruction, write a plan with success criteria for each phase, is doing more work here than any amount of clever prompting would.

One more thing about the plan before we let it run. It made a list of six things to do and it is going to tick them off as it goes, on screen, where you can see it. That list is the single most useful thing on this panel while a build is running.

Because the honest experience of watching an agent work is long stretches where you have no idea whether it is making progress or going in circles. A ticking list is how you tell the difference without reading a line of code.
Then it stopped. Not because anything went wrong, but because it wanted to run a command and it wanted me to say yes first.
One thing that is genuinely different here and worth understanding, because it will shape what you see.
Copilot has a permissions model of its own, and by default it is more cautious than Cursor's. It will ask before it runs terminal commands, and it asks per command rather than per session.

That is more interruption, and it is also more visibility. You see every command before it runs, which for a first build is arguably the better trade. It is the same decision we drew as a ladder two lectures ago, with the dial set one notch tighter.

And I want to be precise about this, because it is the one place today where the tools genuinely diverge, and it is not a small difference. I had already turned auto approve on. It still stopped. It stopped because this particular command installs a package from the internet, and this tool holds that category back no matter what the setting says.
Let me explain what that command actually was, because the word untrusted is doing a lot of work in that sentence and it deserves unpacking.

Modern applications are not written from nothing. They are assembled from thousands of small packages that other people wrote and published, and the command it wanted to run goes off to the internet, downloads a pile of those, and then runs code from them on your machine.

That is completely normal. Every developer does it every day. It is also, genuinely, the largest hole in the side of the boat. If somebody hostile gets code into a popular package, everybody who installs it runs their code. It has happened, more than once, to packages with millions of users.

So a tool that will happily edit your files without asking, but stops and makes you look at the one command that downloads and runs strangers' code, has drawn the line in a defensible place. That is not caution theatre. That is the line I would draw.
And it is worth knowing that the setting you flip to say yes to everything does not override that category. Which is a small design decision that tells you something about the people who built it.

That is a defensible design. Downloading and running somebody else's code is the single riskiest thing an agent does on your machine, and a tool that makes you look at that one is not being annoying, it is being careful. Cursor did not ask me.

It also asked again. And again. Eight times before the build was done, each time showing the exact command, and once showing the exact lines it wanted to change and what they were changing to. That is more interruption than Cursor, and it is also more visibility, and for a first build I would rather have the visibility.
Here is the shape of the next few minutes, and it is the part nobody puts in a demo. It works. It stops and asks. I say yes. It works some more. It stops and asks again.

Eight times, on this build. And each time, the thing it shows you is specific. Here is the exact command I want to run. Here is the exact change I want to make to this file, with the old lines and the new lines side by side.

You do not have to be able to read those lines to get value out of seeing them. What you are checking is much simpler than the code. Is it touching the thing I asked about, or has it wandered somewhere else entirely.
And if you ever see it about to change a file you have never heard of, in a folder you did not know existed, that is your moment. Not later, when it tells you it is finished. Then.

Then it worked. Five columns, all of them renameable. Cards with a title and a description. Drag between columns and reorder inside one, using the browser's own drag handling rather than a library. Seeded data so the board looks alive. And it picked up the colour scheme out of the brief, which nothing forced it to do.
Now let me tell you what it did while I was clicking yes, because two of the six phases are things I did not ask for and did not expect.

Phase four was tests. And I should say plainly what a test is, because the word gets used as though everybody already knows. A test is a small piece of code whose only job is to check that another piece of code does what it should. Move a card from here to there, then ask, is it there.

You write them once and you can run them a thousand times in a couple of seconds. Which means the question is it still working stops being a matter of opinion, or of you clicking around hoping to notice.

It wrote eleven of them for the board logic, and it ran them, and they passed. Nothing in the brief asked for a specific number, or for a specific testing tool. The brief said write tests that can be checked off, and it went and did the whole thing.
Phase five is the one that made me stop and rewind the recording. It started a real browser. Not a simulation of one. An actual browser, running on this machine, which it then drove itself.

It clicked the Add button. It typed into the fields. It picked a card up and dropped it in another column. It shrank the window down to the width of a phone to see whether anything fell off the edge. All of it without me watching, and all of it because the brief mentioned browser verification.

Think about what that is for a second. The thing that wrote the app also wrote the checks for the app, then ran the app, then ran the checks against it, then fixed the two things the checks caught, and then told me it was done.

That is a complete loop with no human in it. And it is the single biggest change in what these tools can do, compared to a year ago, when the same request would have got you a pile of code and a cheerful suggestion that you try running it.
It is also, and I want to put these two sentences next to each other on purpose, the exact reason you should trust its report less rather than more.

Because a tool that writes its own exam, sits its own exam, marks its own exam and then hands you the certificate has not shown you that the app works. It has shown you that it is internally consistent. Those are very different claims, and only one of them is worth anything to you.
So it graded its own homework, and it says it passed.

Which is exactly why we are about to do it again by hand. Not because I think it is lying. Because a tool that tests itself and reports success is making a claim, and the whole discipline of this lecture is that a claim is not a demonstration until you have watched it happen.

One last note on how it looks before we start clicking, because I did not expect this either. It named the thing. It picked a typeface, wrote a headline, and used the colours out of our brief rather than the grey that these builds usually default to.

Nothing in the requirements asked for a name or a headline. The brief said a slick, professional, genuinely good looking interface, and it treated that as a real instruction rather than a nice sentiment. Which is a small lesson about writing briefs, and we will come back to it.
So. Five checks, by hand, on the real thing, the way the person who is going to use it would touch it. Same five as the last build, in the same order, so you can compare like for like.
Drag between columns. The card moves, and the counts on both columns change with it, which is the part a broken version usually gets wrong.
Reorder inside a column. That is a different mechanism from the last one and a very common place for these builds to fall down. It holds.
Delete. Gone, and the count follows it down. This is the one that was broken in the lecture I built this course from, twice, and it is the reason the four step instruction exists at all.
Rename a column. Straight into the heading, no dialogue box, no settings screen.

And add a card. Title, description, and a choice of which column it lands in. Note what this is not. It is not a browser pop up asking for a name with nowhere to put the detail. It is a form, which is what the brief asked for when it said a card has a title and a description.
Five for five, checked by a human, on the free tier, from a small model, off a prompt of four words and a file we wrote two lectures ago.

One technical detail I will name because it shows up in the result and you can see it. The brief said prefer the obvious choice over the clever one, and for dragging things around a screen there is an obvious choice and there is a clever one.

The clever choice is to install a library that specialises in dragging. The obvious choice is to use the dragging that is already built into every browser and has been for years. It took the obvious one, and the result is fewer moving parts and a build that is easier for the next person to change.

That sentence in the brief is nine words long and it changed the shape of the code. This is what I mean when I say the brief is the product. You are not writing wishes, you are setting defaults for a hundred decisions you will never see.

The last thing to say about this build is what it cost, in the two currencies that matter. Under four credits, from a free allowance. And about eleven minutes, most of which I spent clicking yes rather than waiting.

So I have to be honest about the shape of this lecture, because the course I built it from had a different afternoon. There, this build broke. Delete did not work, the agent guessed at a cause, patched it, announced victory, and had not fixed anything. Which is where the four step instruction came from.
Which brings us to the thing this lecture is actually about. Not Copilot. Debugging.

Because when something is broken and you tell an agent it is broken, there is a move it makes almost every single time, and once you have seen it you will never unsee it. It guesses what the problem probably is. It writes a fix for the thing it guessed. And then it tells you the problem is solved.
Two separate things are wrong with that. It should not be guessing, it should be proving. And it should not be claiming a fix it has never once run.

So here is the instruction to give instead, and I would write this one down, because you will use it every week for the rest of your life with these tools. Reproduce the problem. Prove you have reproduced it. Find the root cause. Fix it. Then demonstrate that the fix works.
Four steps, and the order is the whole point. Notice that three of the four are about evidence and only one is about writing code.

And here is the part that matters if you do not write code yourself. You might think that not being a developer means you cannot run that process. It is the opposite. You do not need to read the fix to ask whether it was demonstrated. You are the one who decides that a claim without a demonstration is not finished, and you are allowed to push back even when the answer looks confident and detailed and completely reasonable.
Confident and detailed is what it always looks like. That is not evidence of anything.

Ours did not break, and I am not going to stage a fault to make the lesson land. But do not read our result as the normal one. Write the four steps down anyway, because the first time you are told a bug is fixed and it is not, you will want them already in your hand rather than having to invent them while you are annoyed.
Before the verdict, the part these comparisons normally leave out. Here is what this build did not show you, and it matters more than anything it did show you.

It did not show you a second opinion. Everything on that board is one tool's reading of one brief, on one afternoon. Run it again tomorrow and you will get a different app that also passes all five checks, because there was never one right answer to a brief this loose.

It did not show you what happens when the requirements fight each other. Ours do not. Every line in that brief agrees with every other line, which is not what a real request from a real person looks like. Real ones contain two things that cannot both be true, and nobody notices until something is built.

It did not show you a second day. Nothing here is saved. Close the tab and the board resets, because the brief said no persistence, and the moment you say yes to persistence you have signed up for a database, and accounts, and what happens when two people edit the same card. That is not a bigger version of today. It is a different job.

And it did not show you the thing that actually breaks these projects, which is not code at all. It is a person changing their mind after the thing is built, and nobody having written down what was agreed.

Which, if you have been paying attention, is exactly what the file we spent two lectures on is for. It is not a prompt. It is the written down version of what was agreed, and it is the only artefact from today that would still be useful a month from now.

One practical note on the free allowance, since some of you will hit it. When it runs out, the panel keeps working but the good model stops answering, and you will notice the quality drop before you notice the message explaining it. If a tool suddenly gets worse for no reason, check your usage before you blame the tool.
So let me put the two builds side by side, because two is enough to start seeing a pattern.

Same brief. Same four word prompt. Same five checks. One ran a frontier model I chose by hand. The other ran whatever the free tier handed it. One never asked permission; the other asked eight times. One took eleven minutes of waiting; the other took eleven minutes of clicking yes.
And both of them passed all five checks. Which is not the result I expected when I planned this lecture, and it is the most useful thing in it.

Because the thing people ask before they start is always which one should I buy. And two builds in, the answer looks like it is going to be that on a job this size, with a brief this clear, it genuinely does not matter very much.
Two more to go, and the next one changes shape. It is not really an extension at all, it is a command line tool wearing an editor as a coat, and it is the bridge into everything we do next week.

Before that, though, write the four steps down. Reproduce. Prove. Fix. Demonstrate. Our build behaved today, and the day it does not, that instruction is the difference between an afternoon and a week.
